newsitem.title: INDIA: Politics hold key to Indian shares prospects.
newsitem.headline: Politics hold key to Indian shares prospects.

text.p: Political developments in New Delhi will be the key factor guiding rattled Indian stock markets this week, analysts said.
The markets are expected to rally if a new coalition is cobbled together quickly and investors are assured of some continuity of policies, they said.

India's 10-month old minority government was defeated in a parliamentary confidence vote on Friday. Faced with the threat of snap polls, squabbling politicians were engaged in frantic talks to form a new coalition.

The Congress party, which was responsible for pulling down the government, said on Saturday it would support the United Front coalition provided it removed its leader, ousted prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
"I'm pretty sure a new coalition will be formed," said Ketan Desai, a funds manager at brokerage Asit C. Mehta Investment Intermediates Ltd. "The market's cautiously optimistic."
Holding the markets together was the promise that a much-acclaimed budget, held hostage by the political crisis, would be approved by parliament in a special April 21-23 sitting, analysts said.
But once that is out of the way, the focus would then shift to the uncertainty of political horse-trading, which is expected as a new coalition would be only a stop-gap one, he said.
"Once the budget is passed the market will slide," said Rajesh Bajaj, director at Calcutta brokerage Lohia Securities.
A fractious mandate in last year's national elections gave no single party or group a majority.
The United Front has 178 members, the Congress 140 and the right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its allies 193 in the 545-member Lok Sabha, or lower house of parliament.
The United Front, a centre-left group comprising 15 parties, has said it will not support a Congress or BJP government.
Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) broker Ulhas Paymaster said the market could fall 300-400 points in the event of snap polls.
"It could hurt big players," he said, adding that big investors had accumulated stocks over the past few months in the hope of selling to foreign institutional investors (FIIs).
"The downside risk exists quite a bit. I don't see FIIs chasing prices and moving them higher," Alok Sethi, a director at NatWest Markets told Reuters.
The benchmark BSE index could reach 3,650-3,700 once the budget sets in, he said. On the downside it could sink to 3,100-3,200 if mid-term polls are called.
The index closed last week up 39.35 points, or 1.11 percent, at 3,589.72.
Desai said he believed falling overseas markets would make foreign institutional investors look at India irrespective of the political turmoil.
"For a foreign fund manager there aren't many re-investment opportunities," he said, adding that he expected foreign institutional fund inflows to pick up if valuations become more attractive.
